background.definition: Coccygeal injury encompasses traumatic injuries and nontraumatic pathology resulting in both acute and chronic pain syndromes localized to the coccygeal area. Pain is typically worsened with applied pressure (e.g., sitting).

list.listitem: Trauma (fall) is the most common cause of coccygeal injury.
Other causes include childbirth, neoplasm, avascular necrosis. The cause may also be functional or idiopathic.
The coccyx is the end of the vertebral column. It normally consists of 3 to 5 fused or partially fused segments.

The filum terminale tethers to the coccyx. The coccygeal ligament consists of the filum terminale, surrounded by layers of arachnoid and dura. Nerves of the coccygeal plexus are comprised from S4, S5, and Co branches (twigs), and innervate the skin between the anus and coccyx.
Anterior traction from components of the levator ani musculature provide anterior countertraction to the coccygeal ligament, complicating attempts to reduce coccyx fracture/displacement.

Coccydynia occurs during childbirth (7.3% in one series), with pain occurring as soon as the patient sat after a difficult delivery (use of instruments or describes as difficult by the patient);luxation (i.e. dislocation) was noted in 43.9% of these patients.
Physical examination may reveal ecchymosis in the acute stage, localized sacrococcygeal joint pain, and tenderness and pain with sacrococcygeal motion on rectal examination.
Radiographs are the recommended initial imaging study. Obtain lateral views of the sacrum/coccyx and an AP view of the pelvis.
Diagnosis is usually based on clinical impression and radiologic findings.
Plain films are most commonly used, but may tend to over diagnose coccygeal fracture.

list.listitem: Symptoms of coccygeal injury are more common in women than in men. History of trauma is common, especially a fall onto an object with a projecting edge.

Patients may report pain with sitting, often made worse by slouching in a chair, sitting on a hard surface, or activity. Pain may be aggravated by constipation or rectal disease, and relieved by standing or walking.

Physical examination may reveal ecchymosis in the acute stage. There is also usually localized sacrococcygeal joint pain and tenderness, and there may be pain with sacrococcygeal motion on rectal examination. The pain may radiate into the buttocks.
Maintain a high index of suspicion for related soft tissue and/or other orthopedic injuries.
Radiographs are the recommended initial imaging study. Obtain lateral views of the sacrum/coccyx and an AP view of the pelvis.

Most coccygeal fractures involve the lower sacrum at the S5-Co1 (sacrococcygeal) joint. However, actual fractures are quite uncommon and may be overdiagnosed on plain films by misjudging the normal joint space and angulation as a fracture.
Consider CT scan if radiographs are equivocal and firm coccygeal fracture diagnosis desired.
Suspect coccygeal injury in patients with pain localized in the coccygeal area, especially with acute onset after trauma to the area, such as a fall onto a projecting edge or child birth.
Physical examination may reveal ecchymosis and/or increased pain with coccygeal movement.
Confirm the diagnosis with radiographs; consider CT scan if plain films are normal, but clinical suspicion remains high.
Initial treatment is conservative with analgesics, anti-inflammatories, a donut pillow for sitting, and heat or warm sitz baths. Reduction may be attempted under local anesthesia.
Patients with continuing pain may benefit from localized steroid injections and/or massage.
Selected patients with coccydynia (chronic pain for more than 6 months) may be candidates for surgical referral.
Initial treatment should focus upon pain relief, symptomatic therapy, and patient reassurance.
Realignment may be attempted under local anesthesia, but does not alter the prognosis.
Injection of steroid and a local anesthetic may be considered for patients with chronic pain.
Traumatic coccydynia lasting greater than 6 months may benefit from surgical coccygectomy.
Patients may benefit from acetaminophen, NSAIDs, and other analgesics. Long-term use of narcotics should be avoided.
Chronic pain (coccydynia)and pain resistant to initial medical treatment may respond to injection of steroid plus local anesthetic.

One method is an injection of 40 mg methyl prednisolone acetate plus lidocaine as follows: (a) if pain is increased with manipulation or movement, inject at the SC joint; (b) if pain is from coccygeal tip pressure without movement, inject on either side of coccyx, including the coccygeus muscle.
Another method is to pepper injections of 10 mg Kenalog-40 plus 0.75 mL 2% lidocaine around tender ligament sites.
A third method is a fluoroscopic-guided steroid injection of 80 mg triamcinolone acetate plus 2 mg 1% lidocaine for coccydynia with less than 6 months' duration.
Chronic pain (coccydynia) may necessitate surgical referral, especially in cases of traumatic origin. Recommended time before referral is a minimum of 6 months.
Surgical coccygectomy for coccydynia of traumatic origin has reported success rates ranging from 71% to 100% in case series.

A systematic review identified 21 observatioanl studies with 826 patients who underwent occygectomy for chronic, refractor coccygodynia. Pain scores decreased an average of 5 points on a 10 point scale at 6 to 12 months follow-up and at longer follow-up evaluations. Oswestry disability Index scores also improved in a clinically and statistically significant manner (-23, 95% CI -31 to -15 points). Complications, most often wound dehiscence or infection, occurred in 8% with a 3% reoperation rate.
A study performing partial coccygectomy reported a 93% success rate.
Coccygectomy performed for nontraumatic coccydynia reported a success rates of only 38%, as compared with an 88% success for trauma-induced coccydynia.
Surgical coccygectomy for coccydynia of nontraumatic origin is rarely indicated.
Warm sitz baths, soft donut pillows, and massage and/or manipulation are often recommended, but clinical trials are lacking.
Gluteal muscle exercises are also sometimes recommended: contract gluteal muscles for a count of 5, then release for a count of 5. Repeat this 10 times. Do 3 sets of 10 daily.

Initial therapy may include an attempt to reduce an acute fracture/dislocation under anesthesia; however, there is a high rate of subsequent redisplacement because there is no method to immobilize the fracture site. Realignment has little bearing on the development of coccydynia.

A systematic review identified 10 studies of 515 adults with coccydynia receiving physical therapy. Low quality evidence supported interventions such as massage, manipulation, and levator anus stretching although all studies were short-term.
A small RCT of 51 patients found a small benefit at 1 month following three sessions of intrarectal manipulation.

A review of the literature found no high quality evidence for prolotherapy, steroid injection, nerve blocks, or radiofrequency ablation. They found limited evidence suggesting a benefit of extracorporeal shock wave therapy, stretching, and manipulation.
A small randomized trial (n=34) found that extracorporeal shockwave therapy provided longer lasting pain relief compared with steroid injection.
Fractures tend to become less symptomatic over time; realignment has little bearing on long-term coccydynia.
Traumatic coccydynia may benefit from surgical intervention.
High postsurgical patient satisfaction rates and a low frequency of complications are reported.

Unreduced postfracture ossification of the coccyx may result in anatomic compromise of the obstetric anterior-posterior pelvic outlet diameter, and may necessitate a Cesarean delivery or refracture by obstetrical attendant.
Coccygeal pathology in children often suggests underlying infectious or neoplastic disease. Idiopathic coccydynia and fractures without a history of trauma mandate thorough evaluation.
The most frequent causes of coccygeal disease in children are secondary complications from meningitis or metastatic disease from neoplasms.
Therapy in children should therefore be focused on finding and treating the underlying disease process.

Rising serum alpha-fetoprotein levels can serve as a marker for recurrent malignant sacrococcygeal teratomas. Excision of the primary tumor and coccyx is recommended in all cases of malignant sacrococcygeal teratoma.
